If I include 5 variables, My model is y = beta1*x1 + beta2*x2 + beta3*x3 + beta4*x4.
And I want to add the CAR prior on beta1, beta2, beta3 and beta4, the 4 effects are not independent. And the adjacent matrix is a 4*4 dimension. if my adjacent matrix is as follows:
     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    1    1    1    0
[2,]    1    1    0    0
[3,]    1    0    1    1
[4,]    0    0    1    1

Then the priors is like: beta1 ~ N((beta2+beta3)/2, q^2), beta2 ~  N(beta1, q^2), beta3 ~  N((beta1+beta4)/2, q^2), beta4 ~  N(beta3, q^2), q^2 ~ InvGama(1,1)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: how to add CAR prior on three fixed effect
parts:
Hi,

The length of the index vector has to be the same size of the data, unless you work with projections such the case we have with SPDE models. Specifically, you have to specify to which one of the elements in the graph each observation belongs to. Example: idx1 = rep(1:4, each=25) is the case where the first 25 observations belongs to the first node, the observations from 26 to 50 to the second one, and so on.

Elias

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: how to add CAR prior on three fixed effect
parts:
I agree with Elias, that while your code might now _run_, it doesn't
actually estimate the model you wanted to estimate.

Looking through the thread, I believe what you're looking for are
correlated spatially varying covariate effects.
For simplicity, assuming one observation for each spatial graph node,
and only 3 covariates:

y_i = x_{1i} beta_{1j} + x_{2i} beta_{2j} + x_{3i} beta_{3j} + epsilon_i

where the spatial beta-fields have a kronecker product precision structure,

Q_beta = Q_dependence %x% Q_besag
or
Q_beta = Q_besag %x% Q_dependence

where Q_dependence is related to what you in an earlier email called
"the adjacency matrix" for the beta:s.
(I'm not sure how to turn your "adjacency matrix" into a precision;
need more details of precisely what model you want!)

The second form of the kronecker type model can be implemented using
something like this:

y ~ f(beta_index, covariate_value, model="generic0", Cmatrix=Q_dependence,
group = spatial_index, control.group=list(model="besag", graph
= ..., ...))

where beta_index is
beta_index = rep(1:3, each=spatial_size)
and covariate_value is the vector of covariate values across the
spatial graph, with first all the x_1-values, then the x_2-values,
etc.

PS. This confusion is precisely why Haakon's suggestion in the
beginning of the thread is so important:
When in doubt, or when it's difficult to explain, spell out all the
mathematical details of your model!

Finn

That model has different variance parameters for the different components, which you didn't say anything about before.
But more crucially, it's only part of the picture. The model I described has two "dimensions"; one spatial graph index, and that graph has its own spatial adjacency structure, and one component graph index, and that adjacency describes how the components should connect to eachother instead of being independent.  So when you're talking about "the adjacency", be clear about which of the two you are referring to, and please figure out precisely what joint model for all of this it is you want. We can help with how to implement a given model, but we can't act as general statistical modelling consultants.
We have 3 covariates and 1 observation, so we only have one value of yi. And the y in the formula is the rep(yi, 3)?
Very unlikely. Why would the observations be repeated?
Is beta_index's function telling which covariates belong to each beta?
Yes.
Does Q_dependency mean the precision matrix of beta_1, beta_2 and beta_3?
See above. Q_dependency refers to the at-a-single-spatial-location dependency between the three components.
The spatial size means the number of observation? What is the function of the parameter "group"?

I your number of observations is the same as the number of nodes in the spatial graph, yes. That is entirely up to you and how you want to define your specific model.
group indicates the indexing for the kronecker part of a kronecker precision model.

A more detailed description of a my model is as follows:
I have 3 covariates x1, x2, x3. And I also have beta_1, beta_2 and beta_3. And y = x1*beta_1+x2*beta_2+x3*beta_3.
Please note that this is much much less detailed than what I wrote, since you don't have any of the spatial indexes spelled out.

I want to estimate the value of beta_1, beta_2 and beta_3 using the CAR prior. As for the prior for each beta, is a gaussian distribution where the mean is the average of that beta's neighborhood beta. And the neighborhood is determined by a known adjacent matrix.

I think you mean that their _conditional_ means are the neighbourhood averages? Otherwise you have a simultaneous autoregression model, not a CAR model (except that a SAR model can be written as a second order CAR model, but your book quote described a first order CAR model)

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: how to add CAR prior on three fixed effect
parts:
Thank you for the details, that is much clearer.
Since you don’t want dependence between the beta_k, but just within each of them, you can forget everything I wrote about a group/kronecker model, and probably go back to some of the earlier replies.

Start by constructing a model that just has _one_ beta-field. Adding the others is then just a matter of repeating the same procedure for a new column of your x-covariate matrix.

By definition, from your handwritten note, the beta models do not change over time, so this means you have a fixed player-adjacency matrix across all timepoints (since there is no time-index on beta, only player, and covariate).

Your response variable y should be the vector of all observations.
You will need an “index” vector, saying which player each observation belongs to.
Let x1 be the vector of values from the first column of the covariate matrix for all the players, ordered so that it aligns with the order of the observation vector; if element y[a] is player “i” at time “t”, then x1[a] should be x_{t,1}^i (in the notation of your note).

Define x1_effect = index
The covariate contribution in the formula is then given by
Y ~ f(x1_effect, x1, model=“besag”, ...)

Implement that first. Once you get that to work, add further terms of the same construction for x2, etc, with x2_effect=index, etc.

Finn
